planting.note: Plant grafted or rooted-cutting stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Marumi is among the cold-hardiest kumquat species and tolerates brief dips into the high teens F once established, making it a reliable dooryard or container citrus for Gulf Coast zone 9a.

directions: Marumi is the round-fruited kumquat species, forming a denser, more compact and thornier shrub than the oval-fruited Nagami kumquat. The small, orange-round fruit has a thin, sweet, edible rind wrapped around noticeably tart, seedy pulp, so it is usually eaten whole rather than juiced. The tree is self-fertile and heavy-fruiting even as a young container specimen, and along with Nagami it is one of the parent species behind most modern kumquat hybrids. Feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season and site in the warmest microclimate available in zone 8b-9a, since hard freezes below the high teens can damage wood.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant grafted stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Meiwa is a bit less vigorous and slightly less cold-hardy than Marumi kumquat, so give it the most sheltered spot available in zone 9a or grow it in a movable container.

directions: Meiwa is thought to be a natural hybrid between the round Marumi and oval Nagami kumquats, combining a thicker, sweeter rind with lower-acid, less seedy pulp than either parent, which makes it the kumquat most people prefer for eating fresh out of hand. The nearly thornless, rounded shrub is slightly smaller and less vigorous than standard Nagami, and it bears heavily on short spurs from late fall into winter. It is self-fertile and does well in large containers as readily as in the ground, and like other kumquats it benefits from a citrus-specific fertilizer and a slightly dry rest period before flowering. Whole fruit, rind and all, can be eaten fresh, candied, or preserved.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
Journal of the Japanese Society for Horticultural Science - Phylogeny and Classification of Kumquats (Fortunella spp.)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after frost danger passes; Cuccio (sometimes sold as 'Florida') bears at a notably younger age than many other white sapote selections, which is useful where the growing season for reaching bearing size is shorter.

directions: Cuccio is a light-green-skinned white sapote selection prized for its rich, complex flavor, often described as a blend of peach, pear, banana, caramel, and vanilla, and for holding well on the tree after ripening rather than dropping and bruising immediately. It comes into bearing earlier than many other named white sapote cultivars, making it a good choice for gardeners who want fruit sooner. Plant in deep, well-drained soil sheltered from strong wind, since sapote wood is somewhat brittle, and let harvested fruit finish softening at room temperature for several days before eating. A second white sapote cultivar nearby can improve fruit set, though established trees will produce alone.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers - White Sapote Fruit Facts
growables.org (University of Florida/CRFG archive) - White Sapote Cultivars
University of Florida IFAS Extension - White Sapote Growing in the Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after frost danger passes; Fiesta is a reliable, consistently productive cropper that ripens later than most other named white sapote selections, extending the harvest window into the cooler months.

directions: Selected in Yorba Linda, California in 1973, Fiesta is valued more for dependable, heavy annual cropping than for exceptional size, since its fruit runs noticeably smaller than most other white sapote cultivars at only one to two inches across. It ripens very late in the season, which makes it a useful companion to earlier-fruiting selections like Chestnut or McDill for stretching out the sapote harvest. The tree can set fruit on its own, but planting a second white sapote cultivar nearby generally improves yield and fruit quality. Give it full sun, wind shelter, and well-drained soil, and allow fruit to soften at room temperature after picking before eating.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers - White Sapote Fruit Facts
growables.org (University of Florida/CRFG archive) - White Sapote Cultivars
University of California Cooperative Extension, Ventura County - White Sapote

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after frost danger passes; Malibu is slower to reach bearing age than most other white sapote selections, so gardeners should plan for a longer wait before the first crop.

directions: Developed in Malibu, California in 1981, this selection produces round, yellow fruit that ripens in fall, typically October to November, well after many earlier white sapote cultivars have finished. It takes noticeably longer than average to come into bearing, but growers who plant it consider the wait worthwhile for its rich, custard-like flavor and consistent fall crop once the tree matures. Site it in full sun on deep, well-drained soil with wind protection, since white sapote wood is brittle and prone to breakage in storms. Let harvested fruit soften fully at room temperature for several days, since it does not ripen properly if picked hard and refrigerated.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers - White Sapote Fruit Facts
growables.org (University of Florida/CRFG archive) - White Sapote Cultivars

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Carambola is frost-sensitive (young trees are damaged below 30F and mature trees can be killed near 25F), so in zone 9a give Lara the warmest, most sheltered microclimate available, such as a south-facing wall, or grow it in a movable container.

directions: Lara, selected in Homestead, Florida, is one of the sweet-flavored carambola cultivars recommended by University of Florida IFAS for home landscape planting alongside Arkin. It is notably precocious, fruiting at a young age, and grows into a bushy, rounded tree with attractive deep green foliage that works well as a small specimen or container plant. The waxy, five-ribbed yellow fruit is eaten fresh out of hand or sliced for its familiar star shape as a garnish. Because it shares the frost sensitivity typical of all carambola, Gulf Coast gardeners in zone 9a should plant it in the warmest available spot and be ready to protect young trees during freezes.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension - HS12/MG269 Carambola Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
growables.org (University of Florida archive) - Carambola Varieties

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March-May. Kajang shares the same cold sensitivity as other carambola cultivars, so give it the warmest, most frost-protected microclimate available in zone 9a or grow it in a container that can be moved under cover.

directions: Kajang was among the sweet carambola selections evaluated at the University of Florida's Tropical Research and Education Center and is regarded by many home growers as one of the sweetest, juiciest carambola cultivars available, with large, golden-yellow, crisp-fleshed fruit. The tree tends to stay more compact than standard carambola, which suits smaller yards and container culture. Like all carambola, it is frost-tender and needs a sheltered site in zone 9a, with protection during any hard freeze. Harvest fruit once it has fully colored to deep gold for the best sweetness, since carambola does not continue ripening much after picking.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension - HS12/MG269 Carambola Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
University of Hawaii CTAHR Extension - Carambola General Information
California Rare Fruit Growers - Carambola Fruit Facts
